questions.question: In scaled dot-product self-attention, why is the dot product between queries and keys divided by $\sqrt{d_k}$?
questions.choice_A: To keep the variance of the logits approximately constant across different key/query dimensions, preventing softmax saturation
questions.choice_B: To ensure all attention weights are equal at initialization
questions.choice_C: To reduce computational complexity from $O(n^2)$ to $O(n \log n)$
questions.choice_D: To enforce causality in autoregressive models

questions.question: What is the primary reason for using multiple attention heads in multi-head attention?
questions.choice_A: To reduce the total number of parameters compared to a single head
questions.choice_B: To allow the model to attend to information from different representation subspaces or positions in parallel
questions.choice_C: To avoid the need for positional embeddings
questions.choice_D: To guarantee permutation invariance of the model

questions.question: Which statement best characterizes the roles of keys (K), queries (Q), and values (V) in self-attention?
questions.choice_A: Q selects which tokens to ignore, K stores token positions, and V stores token types
questions.choice_B: Q and K determine attention weights, while V provides the content that is aggregated according to those weights
questions.choice_C: K and V determine attention weights, while Q is aggregated
questions.choice_D: Q, K, and V are interchangeable since they come from the same hidden states

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the purpose of a causal (triangular) attention mask in autoregressive Transformers?
questions.choice_A: It enforces that the total attention weights sum to 1
questions.choice_B: It normalizes the variance across heads
questions.choice_C: It prevents attention across different layers
questions.choice_D: It prevents tokens from attending to future positions, ensuring left-to-right generation

questions.question: What is a key difference between absolute positional embeddings and Rotary Positional Embeddings (RoPE)?
questions.choice_A: Absolute embeddings add position information to token representations, while RoPE rotates query/key vectors in a way that encodes relative positions in their dot products
questions.choice_B: RoPE encodes positions by adding learned bias vectors, while absolute embeddings rotate vectors
questions.choice_C: Absolute embeddings are only used in the feed-forward layers, while RoPE is used only in residual connections
questions.choice_D: RoPE cannot be used in multi-head attention, only single-head attention

questions.question: Why might models with RoPE exhibit better length extrapolation than models with learned absolute positional embeddings?
questions.choice_A: RoPE reduces the number of parameters, preventing overfitting
questions.choice_B: RoPE encodes relative phase relationships in QK dot products, allowing the attention pattern to generalize to positions beyond the training range when appropriately scaled
questions.choice_C: RoPE removes the need for the softmax nonlinearity, making attention more stable
questions.choice_D: Absolute embeddings are incompatible with LayerNorm at long sequence lengths

questions.question: In the standard Transformer feed-forward block, why is the hidden dimension typically larger than the model dimension (e.g., $4\times d_{model}$)?
questions.choice_A: To reduce the parameter count in the attention layers
questions.choice_B: Because it allows parameter sharing across layers
questions.choice_C: To provide a wider nonlinear transformation that increases expressivity before projecting back down
questions.choice_D: To enable weight tying with the embedding matrix

questions.question: What is the main conceptual difference between GLU/SwiGLU and a standard two-layer MLP in Transformer FFNs?
questions.choice_A: GLU/SwiGLU removes nonlinearity entirely
questions.choice_B: GLU/SwiGLU uses convolutional filters, whereas MLP uses linear layers
questions.choice_C: GLU/SwiGLU gates one projection by another (elementwise), enabling multiplicative interactions before projection back
questions.choice_D: GLU/SwiGLU ties weights across layers to improve stability

questions.question: Which of the following is a typical motivation for replacing LayerNorm with RMSNorm in large language models?
questions.choice_A: RMSNorm normalizes only by the root-mean-square, avoiding mean subtraction and often improving training stability and speed with slightly fewer operations
questions.choice_B: RMSNorm enables the model to function without residual connections
questions.choice_C: RMSNorm guarantees better perplexity on any dataset
questions.choice_D: RMSNorm eliminates the need for learning rate warmup

questions.question: What is the practical advantage of pre-norm Transformers (norm before each sub-layer) compared to post-norm (norm after each sub-layer)?
questions.choice_A: Pre-norm completely removes gradient vanishing
questions.choice_B: Pre-norm improves training stability for deep networks by providing smoother gradient flow through residual paths
questions.choice_C: Pre-norm reduces memory usage of activations to zero
questions.choice_D: Pre-norm allows attention to be computed without softmax

questions.question: In multi-head attention, what is the effect of increasing the number of heads while keeping total model dimension fixed?
questions.choice_A: Each head’s key/query/value vectors have smaller dimension, potentially enabling more diverse attention patterns but with less capacity per head
questions.choice_B: The computational cost per token decreases linearly with the number of heads
questions.choice_C: The model becomes invariant to word order
questions.choice_D: The need for positional encodings is eliminated

questions.question: Which architectural ablation is most likely to harm an autoregressive LLM’s ability to remember long-range dependencies during generation?
questions.choice_A: Removing biases from linear projections
questions.choice_B: Replacing LayerNorm with RMSNorm
questions.choice_C: Removing the attention mechanism and keeping only the MLP blocks
questions.choice_D: Changing activation from GELU to ReLU in the MLP

questions.question: What is the primary computational bottleneck of dense self-attention for long sequences of length $n$?
questions.choice_A: Parameter count scales as $O(n^2)$
questions.choice_B: Activation memory scales as $O(n)$
questions.choice_C: Attention compute and memory scale as $O(n^2)$ due to all-pairs token interactions
questions.choice_D: The feed-forward network dominates compute regardless of $n$

questions.question: Which of the following statements about bias terms in Transformer linear projections is most accurate?
questions.choice_A: Bias terms are always necessary for the model to learn non-linear functions
questions.choice_B: Removing biases from Q/K/V and output projections often has negligible effect on quality and can slightly reduce compute and memory
questions.choice_C: Bias terms are only needed in the feed-forward layers, not attention
questions.choice_D: Bias terms are required when using RoPE

questions.question: Why do large-scale LLMs often use weight tying between the token embedding matrix and the output softmax matrix?
questions.choice_A: It guarantees faster inference regardless of hardware
questions.choice_B: It reduces overfitting by dropping parameters and encourages a shared representation between input and output vocabularies
questions.choice_C: It removes the need for normalization layers
questions.choice_D: It allows training without teacher forcing

questions.question: When scaling a Transformer model, which trade-off is best captured by the width vs. depth discussion?
questions.choice_A: Increasing depth generally improves parallelism across layers, reducing latency
questions.choice_B: Increasing width tends to improve per-layer expressivity, while increasing depth improves hierarchical composition; both can yield gains, but optimal allocation depends on data and compute budgets
questions.choice_C: Increasing width always outperforms increasing depth at fixed compute
questions.choice_D: Increasing depth eliminates the need for attention

questions.question: What is the role of the output linear projection (often called W_O) after concatenating all attention heads?
questions.choice_A: It mixes information across heads and maps the concatenated head outputs back to the model dimension
questions.choice_B: It normalizes the output of each head to unit variance
questions.choice_C: It computes positional encodings
questions.choice_D: It enforces causality by zeroing out future positions

questions.question: In the context of KV caching for autoregressive inference, which statement is correct?
questions.choice_A: KV caching stores intermediate MLP activations to save compute
questions.choice_B: KV caching stores past keys and values so that at each new step only the current token’s Q/K/V are computed, avoiding recomputation over the whole prefix
questions.choice_C: KV caching makes attention computation $O(1)$ in sequence length
questions.choice_D: KV caching is incompatible with rotary positional embeddings

questions.question: What is a central motivation for using SwiGLU instead of GELU in the Transformer FFN?
questions.choice_A: SwiGLU drastically reduces FLOPs
questions.choice_B: SwiGLU introduces a gated multiplicative interaction that can improve optimization and downstream performance at similar parameter counts
questions.choice_C: SwiGLU enables exact length extrapolation proofs
questions.choice_D: SwiGLU removes the need for residual connections

questions.question: Which statement best summarizes empirical scaling law insights for LLMs?
questions.choice_A: Test loss improves predictably as a power-law with training compute; there is an approximately optimal trade-off among model size, dataset size, and training steps for a fixed compute budget
questions.choice_B: Loss scaling is unpredictable and unrelated to compute
questions.choice_C: Doubling model size always halves the loss
questions.choice_D: Dataset size does not affect the optimal model size
